title: Correlation Intractability for all Batched Relations
authors: Damiano Abram, Giulio Malavolta, and Lawrence Roy
abstract:
The Fiat-Shamir transform is a central tool in cryptography and understanding its soundness is both a theoretically challenging and practically pressing question. Correlation intractable hash functions offer a method to instantiation Fiat-Shamir in the standard model. In short, a hash function is correlation-intractable for a relation $\mathcal{R}$ if it is computationally hard to find an input $x$ such that $\mathcal{R}(x, \mathsf{Hash}(x)) = 1$.

In this work we present the first construction of a correlation-intractable hash function family, where the complexity of the hash does not depend on the complexity of the relation. Besides being better aligned with the way Fiat-Shamir is used in practice, our construction implies correlation intractability for all (possibly inefficient) batched searchable relations, i.e., searchable relations that can be decomposed as direct product of other searchable relations. Using complexity leveraging, we then compile our construction into correlation intractability for all batched relations. All of our results follow from the hardness of the decomposed short-integer solution (DSIS) problem, the natural search analogue of decomposed LWE, which we show to be at least as hard. 

As a direct consequence from prior work, our result implies that the parallel repetition of any three-message proof cannot be zero-knowledge (unless $\mathrm{BPP} = \mathrm{NP}$).

1       Introduction
The Fiat–Shamir transform [FS87] is a central tool for eliminating interaction from public-coin
protocols. By deriving the verifier’s challenges as the output of a hash function applied to the
prover’s commitment, Fiat–Shamir enables efficient non-interactive proofs and signatures and is
used pervasively in modern cryptographic systems.
    Understanding the security of Fiat–Shamir in the standard model has long been a long-standing
problem. It is known that Fiat–Shamir is not sound in general [GK03] and recent attacks to
practically-deployed protocols [KRS25] underscore the importance of understanding when the trans-
form guarantees soundness. The notion of correlation intractability [CGH98] was proposed as a
unifying abstraction capturing some of the properties required of the hash function in Fiat–Shamir.
For a binary relation R(x, y), a hash family (Setup, Hash) is correlation-intractable for R if, given a
                   $
hash function hk ← Setup, it is computationally hard to find an input x such that R(x, Hash(hk, x))
is true. For this definition to be achievable, we additionally require that the relation R is sparse:
for any x, all but a negligible fraction of y do not satisfy the relation with x. A typical example
are searchable relations, where there exists a function f such that, for every x, (x, y) ∈ R only if
y = f (x). We say that the relation is efficiently searchable if f is efficiently computable.

    In recent years, there has been substantial progress in constructing correlation-intractable hash
functions for efficiently searchable relations [CCR16, KRR17, CCRR18, HL18, CCH+ 19, PS19,
LV22] and even the Cartesian product of efficiently-checkable relation [HLR21]. This paradigm has
lead to enormous advances in establishing the security of cryptographic protocols in the standard
model, leading to new constructions of non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs [PS19, JJ21], batch
[CJJ21, DGKV22, PP22], and succinct [CJJ22, KLVW23, BBK+ 23] arguments, to mention a few.
    Nevertheless, our understanding of the Fiat-Shamir transformation remains limited: for one, the
complexity of all known correlation-intractable hashes in the standard model scales with the time
needed to check the relation. While this is seemingly a technical point, there are multiple reasons
why this aspect is unsatisfactory: (i) for starters, it places a lower bound on the concrete efficiency of
the hash function, moreover (ii) it limits correlation-intractability to efficiently searchable relations,
whereas interactive protocols use in practice do no necessarily enjoy this property. Finally, (iii) it
does not reflect how the Fiat-Shamir transform is used in real-world protocols, where the complexity
of the hash is typically independent of that of the underlying protocol.
    Taken together, the above limitations underscore our lack of understanding of the soundness
of the Fiat-Shamir transform, which is one of the most pressing problem in the theory of modern
cryptography. The goal of this work is to make progress on this question.

1.1   Our Results
In this work we propose a construction of correlation intractable hash functions for all batched
relation, i.e., relations that consist of the direct product of other relations
                                       R := R(0) × · · · × R(c−1) .
We do not place any computational restriction on the relations that we consider, with the only
constraint being that c must be a sufficiently large polynomial in the security parameter. In
particular, we obtain the first correlation intractability hash functions for not efficiently searchable
relations.
    A necessary condition for this to be possible is that the complexity of our hash function cannot
depend on the complexity of the relation R. Thus, in order to achieve our main result, we need
to overcome a technical barrier present in, as far as we are aware, all prior work on correlation
intractability in the standard model. In the batched settings, this answers affirmatively an open
question by Lombardi [Lom25].
    We prove that our hash function family is correlation intractable assuming the (sub-exponential)
hardness of the decomposed short integer solution (DSIS) problem, a problem that which we intro-
duce in this work. DSIS is the natural search analogue of the decomposed LWE problem [AMR25a]
and in this work we show that it is at least as hard as decomposed LWE. In turn, it is known that
the hardness of the decomposed LWE problem is implied by the hardness of the succinct LWE
problem [Wee24, AMR25a].
    We summarize our results with the following theorem statement.
Theorem 1 (Informal). Assuming the sub-exponential hardness of the DSIS problem, there exists
a correlation-intractable hash functions for all batched relations.

basic construction for batched searchable relations from decomposed SIS ; then, we use complexity
leveraging to compile the basic solution into a correlation intractable hash function for all batched
relations.

An Issue with Compactness. Unfortunately, the construction described above has a funda-
mental problem, namely that the hash function is not compressing. Indeed, the norm of the SIS
solution h0 , h1 , h2 increases proportionally to the space complexity of F . That means that in order
to achieve correlation intractability we need q > L and so n = k log q > log L. Designing correlation
intractability for non-compressing functions is trivial: just use the constant function that outputs
an element that is outside of the image of f .
    Nevertheless our construction has two desirable properties. (i) The first one is that hashing
and generating the key requires time poly(λ, log L), so one can, in principle, instantiate our con-
struction with a superpolynomial L, e.g., 2ℓ . Notice that this would require the reduction to run
in superpolynomial time (the evaluation of F requires time proportional to L), but in the technical
section we show that using a recent variant of the compressed encodings [AMR26] we can actually
homomorphically evaluate F in time T · poly(λ, log L) where T is the complexity of f . (ii) The
second interesting property is that the parameters of the hash functions only depend polylogarith-
mically on the time complexity of f (this is because the norm of the SIS solution h0 , h1 , h2 increases
proportionally to the time complexity of F , and the dependency is inherited by the modulus q).
Therefore, assuming the subexponential hardness of DSIS, we can prove that our hash function
is correlation intractable even for searchable relations where f is inefficient. To make our result
interesting, we just need to find a way to achieve compression.

Correlation Intractability for Batched Searchable Relations. To understand how to solve
the issue, let us take a step back and compare with known approaches. Previous constructions of
correlation intractability [PS19, LV22, BKM20] computationally hid the description of the function
f in the key, so that, hashing x, the attacker would obliviously compute f (x) + PRFK (x). Then,
they argued that with overwhelming probability over K, 0 is not in the image of PRFK . In such
case, there exists no x such that f (x) = Hash(hk, x) = f (x) + PRFK (x). Notice that this would
intrinsically require the complexity of the hash function to grow proportionally to that of f .
     Our approach instead differs in two ways. First of all, the reduction hides the description of
f in the hash key information theoretically, and we rely on a computational argument to argue
that finding an x such that PRFK (x) = 0 is hard. Second, we split the computation of f (x) into
two parts: an input-independent, inefficient preprocessing that is performed by the reduction and
hidden in the hash key (this corresponds to the homomorphic computation of the truth table of
f ), and a lightweight computation that depends on x which is performed in encrypted way by
the hasher (this roughly corresponds to homomorphically read the x-th entry of the truth table).
This ensures that the complexity of the hash function is independent of that of f , indeed, there
is only a polylogarithmic dependence on the time and space complexity of the computation that
the reduction embeds in the key. Unfortunately, in the construction we illustrated, these scale
proportionally to L, therefore exponentially in the length of the input x!
     What happens, however, if we consider a different class of functions, where the evaluation of f on
x can be split into an inefficient input-independent preprocessing with subexponential complexity
in the length of the input, and a lightweight computation that depends on x, but not on f ? Our
recipe is likely to give a correlation intractable hash function for a non-trivial class of inefficiently
searchable relations.

equal length and we tackle the relation Rf c where

7    The Parallel Repetition of 3-Round Proofs is Not Zero-Knowledge
As a consequence of our main result, the parallel repetition (for a sufficiently large number of repe-
titions) of any three-round proof is not zero-knowledge. This follows by the well-known connection
between correlation intractability and zero-knowledge [DNRS99, HLR21]. For completeness, we
recall the argument here, but this implication can also be found explicitly in [HLR21].
     A three-round proof Π between a prover and a verifier for a language L satisfies c-completeness
if for all x ∈ L the probability that the transcript (α, β, γ) is accepting is at least c = c(λ). For the
special case of three-round proofs we can define the s-soundness as follows: For all x ∈      / L and all
first messages α, it holds that

                                   Pr [∃ γ : (α, β, γ) ∈ Accept] ≤ s
                                    β

for some function s = s(λ). Then we say that the protocol is non-trivially sound if c−s ≥ 1/poly(λ).
The following claim is a restatement from [DNRS99, HLR21]. The original proof considers the case
of completeness-soundness gap negligibly close to 1, but the proof works almost in verbatim for the
case of a non-trivial gap. We recall the proof for completeness.

Lemma 4 ([DNRS99, HLR21]). Assume that there exists a function family (Setup, Hash) and a
three-round protocol Π for a language L such that, with all but negligible probability over the choice

of hk ← Setup(1λ ), the protocol with β = Hash(hk, (x, α)) is non-trivially sound. If the three-round
protocol is zero-knowledge, then L ∈ BPP.

Sketch. Consider a verifier that is given as an auxiliary input a function hk ← Setup(1λ ) and that
computes β = Hash(hk, (x, α)). Then by assumption there must exist a simulator that, for all x ∈ L
produces an accepting transcript that is computationally indistinguishable from the honest run of
a protocol. Then we consider the distinguisher that simply checks if β was computed correctly and
if the transcript is accepting. We have two cases:

    • x ∈ L: In this case the distinguisher accepts with probability negligibly close to c, since
      the simulator must produce a transcript that is computationally indistinguishable from the
      original one, and the honest transcript accepts with probability c.

    • x∈/ L: In this case the distinguisher accepts with probability at most s since, by assumption,
      the protocol is sound with β computed as the output of the hash.

Since the original protocol is non-trivially sound, the advantage of the distinguisher is at least
inverse-polynomial.

    Thus, we obtain the following consequence. Let Π be any three round protocol for a language
not in BPP. Then its c-fold parallel repetition, for a sufficiently large c = poly(λ), defines a batched
relation. Combining Lemma 4 with Corollary 2, we obtain that the parallel repeated protocol is
not zero-knowledge.
